title: Tropic Trooper
summary: Tropic Trooper, also reported as Pirate Panda and KeyBoy, is a long-running espionage cluster that public reporting describes targeting government, healthcare, research, retail and transport organisations in Taiwan and the Philippines, with activity tracked from around 2011 onward. Trend Micro and other vendors documented repeated use of weaponised documents that exploited unpatched office software, combined with backdoors that treated removable drives as a delivery and collection channel, letting the operators copy files and move tools across air gapped or weakly connected machines. Later reporting showed the group adopting legitimate remote access services and public cloud storage for command and control. The persistence of the campaign is explained less by sophistication than by slow patching and by the difficulty of monitoring removable media, which makes patch governance and device control the practical defensive priorities.

beginner.definition: Tropic Trooper is a spying group that has attacked organisations in Taiwan and the Philippines for many years. It sent documents that opened harmful code when the reader clicked. It also used USB drives, which are small portable storage devices, to move files between computers. Some reports call the same activity Pirate Panda or KeyBoy. The group is not very advanced, but it keeps trying for a long time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Old, unpatched software is still a working way into a network. The group also used USB drives to reach computers that had no internet connection. Many teams forget those machines entirely. Free cloud storage and remote support services were used to hide messages, and those look harmless in logs. So patching, control of portable drives and review of cloud sign-ins all matter here.
howItWorks: The attackers send a document that uses a weakness in outdated office software.
When the reader opens the document, the harmful code starts on the computer.
A backdoor stays on the machine and waits for instructions from the attackers.
It copies files to a USB drive when someone plugs one into the computer.
The drive then carries the tool to other machines, including ones that are kept offline.
The attackers also use normal cloud services to send and receive data quietly.
beginner.example: Think of an office where the front gate is checked, but staff carry documents home on memory sticks. A visitor cannot get past the gate, so instead he slips a note into a colleague's bag at the bus stop. The note travels inside, past every check, and comes back out the same way. Whatever leaves the building must be inspected too.
takeaways: Unpatched office software remains a common way in, so keep updates moving.
Removable drives can carry files out of your network, so control their use.
Watch sign-ins to cloud services for accounts that should not use them.

objectives: Explain why patch management is a primary control against document based attacks.
Describe how removable media can move data into and out of a network.
Explain what a backdoor is and why it stays quiet for long periods.
Recognise how ordinary cloud services can be used for command and control.
Outline a simple device control policy for portable storage.
